kurals.tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறுஇலவாம்
செம்பொருள் கண்டார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Insolaal eeram alaiip padiru ilavaam,
Semporul kandaarvaaich chol.
kurals.meaning: Truly sweet words are the words that come from the mouths of those who have grasped what is genuinely right — words steeped in warm affection and entirely free of deceit.
kurals.elementary: Kind words are like real honey, not sugar water that only looks sweet. Some people say nice things but are secretly trying to trick you. This kural says real sweet talk has two ingredients: it has to be warm and loving, and it has to be honest. If either one is missing, it isn't the real thing.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining his terms, a move typical of his method. The Tamil packs three conditions into a single couplet: ஈரம் (eeram, literally 'moistness' — the warmth or tenderness of a heart that is not dry), படிறு இல (padiru ila, 'without guile or fraud'), and செம்பொருள் கண்டார் (semporul kandaar, 'those who have seen the straight/true substance'). Sweet speech is therefore not a rhetorical technique but a moral by-product: it issues from a particular kind of person. This explicitly rules out flattery, the counterfeit that classical ethical traditions across Eurasia were equally anxious to distinguish from genuine kindness — the Tamil padiru occupies almost exactly the space that Greek kolakeia (flattery) and Sanskrit anrta (falsehood in speech) occupy in their respective systems. Placing this definition first also protects the whole remaining chapter from being read as advice on charm or social technique.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu prescribes a fourfold rule for speech: it must be both true and pleasant, and neither quality may be purchased at the cost of the other.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact double requirement — words mixed with affection (pleasing) and free of guile (true) — stated as a single legal maxim.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 4.138 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Bühler's translation; the correspondence is close to one-to-one, including the explicit rejection of 'agreeable falsehood' (= padiru).

christianity.quote_or_event: “But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Ephesians that Christian maturity requires holding truth and love together rather than trading one off against the other.
christianity.tie_back: Same fusion the Kural demands: the word must carry affection (eeram) and must be true (free of padiru).
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the phrase 'truth in love' matches the Kural's two conditions precisely, though Paul's frame is ecclesial growth rather than general ethics.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'anic phrase qawlan sadidan denotes speech that is straight, sound and upright — the opposite of crooked or self-serving talk.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's insistence that sweet speech must proceed from someone aligned with what is genuinely right (semporul).
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sahih International wording, but the verse stresses uprightness of speech without the Kural's explicit note of tenderness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes betrayal by a close companion whose speech was deliberately soothing while his intent was hostile.
judaism.tie_back: It is the exact negative image of the Kural: the outward sweetness is present, but the eeram is absent and padiru fills the gap.
judaism.source: Psalms 55:21 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; a strong thematic match but expressed as a portrait of deceit rather than a positive definition, and quoted here via a Christian translation of the Tanakh.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is spoken at the right time. It is spoken in truth. It is spoken affectionately. It is spoken beneficially. It is spoken with a mind of good-will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the five marks of a statement that is 'well-spoken' and therefore blameless in the eyes of the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Truth and affection appear side by side in the Buddhist list exactly as they do in the Kural's definition of insol.
buddhism.source: Vācā Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.198 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; the five factors subsume both of Valluvar's conditions and add timing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then among them arose Nestor, sweet of speech, the clear-voiced orator of the Pylians, from whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer introduces Nestor at the height of the Achaean quarrel; his authority rests not on force but on speech that is at once honeyed and trustworthy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nestor personifies the Kural's claim that genuinely sweet words belong to those who have perceived what is right.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 1.247–249 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus; an exemplary figure rather than a stated principle, and Homer does not thematise guilelessness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part … And thou must do this neither with any double meaning nor in the way of reproach, but affectionately and without any rancour in thy soul.”
philosophy.explanation: Among his rules for dealing with people who give offence, Marcus Aurelius says kindness only has power when it is real: speech must come from genuine affection and carry no hidden meaning or concealed ill-will.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s sweet words are likewise defined by being steeped in affection and free of deceit, not by being pleasant on the surface.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §18 (ninth rule) (tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Strong match on affection without guile; the Kural's further point that such words come from people who have grasped what is right is only implicit in Marcus's Stoic context.

kurals.tamil:
அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே முகனமர்ந்து
இன்சொலன் ஆகப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aganamarndhu eedhalin nandre muganamarndhu,
Insolan aagap perin.
kurals.meaning: To have a face that lights up and a tongue that speaks kindly is better still than giving a gift with a heart full of goodwill.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two people give you a birthday present. One hands it over without looking up. The other is grinning, says your name, and tells you they hoped you'd like it. The second present feels bigger — even if it cost less. This kural says the warm face and the kind words are worth more than the gift itself.
kurals.university: The couplet sets up a deliberate comparison between two goods that the previous chapters have already praised: ஈதல் (eedhal, giving) and இன்சொல் (insol, sweet speech). Valluvar does not dismiss generosity; he ranks a cheerful countenance and kind word above even generosity offered with an expanded heart (அகன் அமர்ந்து, agan amarndhu — 'the inner self settled in gladness'). The wordplay is structural: அகன் அமர்ந்து (inner gladness) is answered by முகன் அமர்ந்து (mugan amarndhu, 'face settled in gladness'), so the verse argues that the outward, relational expression completes what the inward disposition begins. This ordering — manner above material — is one of the most widely paralleled ideas in world ethical literature, appearing almost verbatim in Ben Sira and in the rabbinic calculus of blessings attached to charity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In its closing charge to departing students, the Taittiriya Upanishad rules that a gift must be given with faith, never without faith, given in abundance, given with modesty, given with a kind of awe, and given with fellow-feeling — the manner of giving being legislated as carefully as the giving itself.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad's convocation address treats dāna not as a transfer of goods but as a relational act whose inner and outward bearing determine its worth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the value of a gift in the warmth and bearing that accompany it rather than in the object handed over.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verified passage; it elevates the manner of giving but stops short of the Kural's explicit ranking of word above gift.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Shall not the dew asswage the heat? so is a word better than a gift. Lo, is not a word better than a gift? but both are with a gracious man.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira compares a kind word to dew cooling the heat of the day and states outright that it surpasses a material present, while noting the generous person offers both.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis almost word for word: the kind word ranks above the gift.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the KJV Apocrypha; one of the closest single-verse parallels to any Kural in this chapter.

islam.quote_or_event: “Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks a gentle word above almsgiving that is spoiled by reproach or humiliation of the recipient.
islam.tie_back: Identical ordering to the Kural: the sweet word outweighs the material gift.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the Qur'an's comparison is with flawed charity, slightly narrower than the Kural's comparison with wholehearted giving.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that one who gives a coin to a poor person receives six blessings, but one who consoles him with words receives eleven — the count drawn from successive verses of Isaiah 58.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud quantifies the difference, using scriptural proof-texts to show that comforting speech outranks the coin nearly two to one.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim rendered as an arithmetic: the kind word is worth more than the gift.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verified passage (wording varies by translation); the substantive match is nearly exact.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the four saṅgahavatthu — the 'bases of sympathy' by which a person binds a community together — the Buddha places dāna (giving) and peyyavajja (kindly speech) side by side, followed by beneficial conduct and impartiality.
buddhism.explanation: Kindly speech is listed as a full social virtue in its own right, not as an accessory to generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: It puts the kind word on the same footing as the gift, though without the Kural's explicit ranking of one above the other.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of a canonical list, but Buddhism pairs the two rather than ranking speech above giving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an aged and desperately poor couple, are the only people in their district to welcome Zeus and Hermes travelling in disguise; they have almost nothing to offer but receive the strangers with delighted faces, bustling warmth and constant talk, and are rewarded while their wealthy neighbours are destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's point turns entirely on manner: the gods are honoured by the couple's gladness, not by the value of the meal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's ranking — the beaming face and warm words outweigh what is materially given.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Faithful summary of the episode; the parallel is real but inferred from narrative rather than stated as a maxim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues throughout On Benefits that the benefit is never the coin or the object but the goodwill behind it, and that a favour delivered grudgingly — with frowning brows and muttered words — is like a stone thrown at a hungry man instead of bread.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca the gift is merely the visible trace of a benevolent intention; a harsh manner cancels it entirely.
philosophy.tie_back: It supports the Kural's ranking: what is actually received by the other person is the manner, not the material.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Beneficiis (On Benefits), Books I–II
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Seneca's recurring argument rather than a single verified line; English renderings of the 'stony bread' image vary widely by translator.

kurals.tamil:
முகத்தான் அமர்ந்துஇனிது நோக்கி அகத்தானாம்
இன்சொ லினதே அறம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mugatthaan amarndhu inidhu nokki agatthaanaam,
Inso linadhe aram.
kurals.meaning: A face that welcomes, a gaze that rests kindly on the other person, and sweet words that come up from inside rather than off the surface — that itself is virtue.
kurals.elementary: When someone talks to you while looking at their phone, even nice words feel cold. But when a person turns to you, smiles, actually looks at you, and means what they say — that feels completely different. This kural says that whole package isn't just being polite. It IS being good.
kurals.university: The couplet is structured as an ascending sequence of three organs of kindness: முகத்தான் (mugatthaan, by the face), நோக்கி (nokki, by the look), and அகத்தான் (agatthaan, from within). The claim in the final word is unusually strong — Valluvar does not say such conduct leads to அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) or is a part of it, but that it is aram, full stop. Given that aram is the governing category of the entire first book of the Kural, encompassing householder duty, ascetic restraint and social justice, identifying it with a warm face and a heartfelt word is a striking democratisation of virtue: it makes the moral life available in every ordinary encounter, requiring neither wealth nor renunciation. The insistence that the word must arise அகத்தான் — from the interior — also forecloses the reading that this is mere etiquette.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies pleasant, non-agitating speech as a form of tapas — spiritual discipline — placing it on the same plane as bodily and mental austerity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats gentle speech not as social lubricant but as a religious practice in its own right.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the standard As It Is rendering; elevates speech to austerity, matching the Kural's elevation of it to aram, though without the facial/visual elements.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs traces the visible face directly back to the inner state, treating the countenance as an honest readout of the heart.
christianity.tie_back: It underwrites the Kural's chain from within (agatthaan) to the face (mugatthaan).
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; it describes the heart–face link the Kural assumes but does not make the moral claim that this constitutes virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not belittle any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks a welcoming expression as a genuine act of ma'ruf (good), not a trivial courtesy.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim exactly: the welcoming face is itself moral action, not a preliminary to it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified against Sunnah.com; wording is the standard English rendering and the conceptual match is near-exact.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Make your Torah fixed, say little and do much, and receive every person with a cheerful countenance.”
judaism.explanation: Shammai, famously the stricter of the two great first-century sages, nonetheless makes a welcoming face one of his three foundational rules of conduct.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's mugatthaan amarndhu — the settled, glad face turned toward the other — is precisely Shammai's sever panim yafot.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified against Sefaria; the match on the facial element is exact, though Shammai does not add the Kural's claim about the inner source of speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind is the forerunner of all states... If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts, happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening pair establishes that speech and action take their entire moral quality from the mental state that generates them.
buddhism.tie_back: It grounds the Kural's insistence that the sweet word must come agatthaan — from within — to count as virtue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Buddharakkhita's wording, quoted with an ellipsis; addresses the interiority condition precisely but not the face or gaze.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names the three Charites — Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia — daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, from whose glancing eyes a melting sweetness flows; they are the goddesses who make gracious social exchange possible, and Greek thought derived the whole vocabulary of charis (grace, favour, gratitude) from them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Graces divinise exactly the cluster the Kural lists: the warm look, the pleasing manner, the reciprocity of goodwill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They mythologise the gaze and countenance the Kural names as the outward face of virtue.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate summary, but Greek myth personifies social charm without making the Kural's moral identification of it with virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such as a man's character is, he immediately shows it in his eyes, just as he who is beloved forthwith reads everything in the eyes of lovers … The good and simple and benevolent show all these things in the eyes, and there is no mistaking.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius mocks the man who announces that he means to deal fairly, saying real goodness needs no announcement because it shows itself at once in a person’s eyes and bearing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise locates virtue in the welcoming face and kindly gaze, and treats these as outward signs of what is inside rather than as decoration.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §15 (tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Close on the face and eyes showing inner goodness; Marcus does not mention sweet speech, which is the Kural's third element.

kurals.tamil:
துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை இல்லாகும் யார்மாட்டும்
இன்புறூஉம் இன்சொ லவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunburooum thuvvaamai illaagum yaarmaattum,
Inburooum inso lavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Those who speak words that gladden everyone they meet, without exception, will never be overtaken by the grinding poverty that brings misery.
kurals.elementary: Think of someone at school everybody likes because they're kind to everyone — not just their own friends. When that person needs help, ten people offer. Being warm to everybody builds up a kind of invisible savings account. This kural says people like that don't end up with nothing.
kurals.university: The key word is யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, 'toward anyone at all'), which universalises the obligation and rules out selective charm directed at the useful. துவ்வாமை (thuvvaamai) is a striking choice: it derives from துவ்வு (to eat/enjoy) and so denotes destitution specifically as the inability to consume or enjoy — want at the level of the body. Valluvar claims that the person who gives everyone the enjoyment (இன்புறூஉம், inburooum) of a kind word will not suffer the want of enjoyment. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward have read this both prudentially (goodwill converts into material support) and karmically (the merit of universal kindness bears fruit). The verse also uses the elongated alapedai forms துன்புறூஉம் / இன்புறூஉம் to set the two states of misery and delight in exact metrical opposition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely transmitted Sanskrit maxim states that all creatures are gratified by the giving of pleasing words, and therefore one should speak only in that way — asking, pointedly, 'where is the poverty in words?'
hinduism.explanation: The verse notes that kind speech is the one currency that never runs out, so there can be no economic excuse for withholding it.
hinduism.tie_back: It joins kind speech directly to the vocabulary of poverty (daridratā), exactly as the Kural joins insol to thuvvaamai.
hinduism.source: Subhāṣita, attributed to Chāṇakya Nīti 16.13 (also collected in the Subhāṣita Ratna Bhāṇḍāgāra)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Source attribution verified; rendered as paraphrase because English translations of this subhāṣita vary considerably and no single canonical version exists.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs links a pure heart and gracious speech to concrete advancement — securing the favour of the most powerful patron available.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the Kural's prudential claim that gracious speech protects a person from destitution.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the mechanism (royal favour) is narrower and more courtly than the Kural's universal 'toward anyone at all'.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that every good word is itself an act of charity (sadaqah), placing speech within the same economy of giving and reward as almsgiving.
islam.explanation: The hadith reclassifies speech as a transferable good, so the person with nothing to give materially is never actually empty-handed.
islam.tie_back: It supports the Kural's link between kind speech and freedom from want by making the kind word a form of wealth.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2989 (Book of Jihad, chapter on charity)
islam._accuracy_note: Rendered as paraphrase because the phrase appears in several hadith collections with differing wording; the underlying teaching is well attested.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Sweet language will multiply friends: and a fairspeaking tongue will increase kind greetings.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira presents pleasant speech as an investment that compounds: it generates a widening circle of allies and reciprocal goodwill.
judaism.tie_back: This is the practical mechanism behind the Kural's promise that the kind speaker will not fall into destitution.
judaism.source: Ben Sira / Ecclesiasticus 6:5 (King James Version, Apocrypha)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim including the KJV's 'fairspeaking'; promises abundance of friends rather than explicitly freedom from poverty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Maṅgala Sutta, the Buddha's catalogue of the highest blessings (maṅgala) available in a human life, lists well-spoken speech alongside vast learning, mastered discipline and skilled craft as among the things that make a life auspicious and secure.
buddhism.explanation: Pleasant, well-formed speech is counted as an actual component of worldly good fortune, not merely of moral character.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that kind speech produces the good fortune that keeps misery-bringing want at bay.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of a canonical list; 'blessing' is broader and vaguer than the Kural's specific promise about poverty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...they pour sweet dew upon his tongue, and from his lips flow gracious words.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the Muses' gift to a king they favour at birth: his gracious speech settles disputes, and in consequence the whole people look to him and he is conspicuous in the assembly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It ties honeyed speech directly to standing and security, the same causal link the Kural draws.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Evelyn-White; the reward is prestige and authority rather than freedom from poverty, and the gift is divinely bestowed rather than earned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Acquire the Reputation of Courtesy; for it is enough to make you liked. Politeness is the main ingredient of culture,—a kind of witchery that wins the regard of all as surely as discourtesy gains their disfavour and opposition...”
philosophy.explanation: Gracián, writing a manual of worldly survival for the seventeenth-century court, treats courtesy as the cheapest and most reliable instrument of advantage available to anyone.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural's prudential argument stated frankly: kind speech is what keeps a person from being left with nothing.
philosophy.source: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, §118 (trans. Joseph Jacobs, 1892)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Jacobs translation; Gracián's motive is frankly strategic, where Valluvar's is moral, so the tone diverges even though the prediction matches.

kurals.tamil:
பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல் ஒருவற்கு
அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Panivudaiyan insolan aadhal oruvarku,
Aniyalla matrup pira.
kurals.meaning: To be humble and to speak kindly — that is a person's real ornament; nothing else deserves the name.
kurals.elementary: You can put on the nicest shoes and the coolest jacket and still have nobody want to sit with you. But if you're kind and you don't act like you're better than everyone, people want to be near you. This kural says humility and kind words are the jewellery that actually works.
kurals.university: அணி (ani) in Tamil poetic usage covers both physical ornament and rhetorical figure, so Valluvar's metaphor carries a faint irony: the true 'figure of speech' is not an embellishment of language but a quality of the speaker. The pairing of பணிவு (panivu, humility/bending) with இன்சொல் is deliberate — sweet speech without humility collapses into condescension, while humility without kind speech remains invisible. The closing அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற ('other things are not ornaments') is an absolute exclusion, and Tamil commentators note it as a rejection of the courtly display culture in which jewellery signified rank. The trope of speech-as-the-only-true-ornament is remarkably widespread: Bhartrihari's Sanskrit formulation is so close that some comparatists have argued for shared circulation of the image across the Deccan in the early centuries CE, though no dependency can be demonstrated.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari writes that armlets do not adorn a person, nor necklaces bright as the moon, nor bathing, nor perfumes, nor flowers, nor dressed hair — one thing alone adorns a person, and that is cultivated speech; all other ornaments perish, but the ornament of speech is the enduring ornament.
hinduism.explanation: The verse works through a catalogue of conventional finery and dismisses each in turn before naming refined speech as the sole real adornment.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim in almost identical terms, including the explicit denial that anything else counts as an ornament.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verse and content verified; given as paraphrase because English translations vary widely and no standard version is canonical.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: 1 Peter contrasts visible finery with an inward disposition of meekness, and names the latter the genuinely valuable ornament.
christianity.tie_back: Same metaphor, same exclusion, and the same pairing of humility with the true ornament.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the ornament named is meekness of spirit rather than speech specifically, but the humility half maps exactly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an's portrait of the ideal believer fuses humility of bearing with gentleness of speech, even under provocation.
islam.tie_back: It names the Kural's exact pair — humility plus kind speech — as the defining marks of the highest human type.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the two qualities are joined exactly as in the Kural, though the ornament metaphor is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yishmael taught that one should be yielding to a superior, pleasant and easy toward the young, and should receive every person with gladness.
judaism.explanation: The maxim binds deference upward, gentleness downward and warmth in all directions into a single rule of bearing.
judaism.tie_back: It couples humility with pleasant speech exactly as the Kural does, as the whole of a person's proper adornment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, since English renderings of the term for 'yielding/suave' differ substantially; the pairing of humility and pleasantness is secure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada repeatedly dismisses outward religious markers — matted hair, animal-skin robes, ritual bathing — as worthless while the interior remains impure, insisting that the only real distinction is an inward one.
buddhism.explanation: The verses attack the assumption that visible tokens can stand in for the cultivated qualities they are supposed to signify.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's logic that external adornments are not ornaments at all; only inner quality is.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as translations of these verses diverge; the target is religious pretension rather than social ornament, so the fit is partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For one man is inferior in comeliness, but the god sets a crown of beauty upon his words, and men look upon him with delight, and he speaks on unfalteringly with sweet modesty, and is conspicuous among the gathered people, and as he goes through the city men gaze upon him as upon a god.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Stung by a young Phaeacian's mockery of his unimpressive appearance, Odysseus replies that the gods distribute gifts unevenly and that gracious, modest speech outshines physical beauty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis dramatised: speech joined to modesty is the adornment that actually makes a person admired.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.169–175 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus; 'sweet modesty' (aidoi meilichiē) captures both of the Kural's terms, though framed as divine gift rather than cultivated virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Politeness is to human nature what warmth is to wax.”
philosophy.explanation: Schopenhauer's point is that courtesy softens people who are otherwise rigid and hostile, making them workable — a small expenditure with disproportionate effect.
philosophy.tie_back: It backs the Kural's claim that humble, kind speech is the one quality that genuinely does the work other displays only pretend to.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, Counsels and Maxims, ch. III 'Our Relation to Others', §36
philosophy._accuracy_note: Quotation verified and located, but Schopenhauer's interest is instrumental (managing people) rather than the Kural's claim about what adorns a person.

kurals.tamil:
அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும் நல்லவை
நாடி இனிய சொலின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Allavai theya arampperugum nallavai,
Naadi iniya solin.
kurals.meaning: If a person searches out what is genuinely good to say and then says it pleasantly, evil wears away and virtue grows.
kurals.elementary: It's like weeding a garden. Every time you plant something good — a kind, helpful word — there's a little less room for weeds. Do it often enough and the weeds shrink while the flowers spread. This kural says kind, useful words work on the world like that.
kurals.university: The verb நாடி (naadi, 'having sought out, investigated') is the hinge of the couplet and is easy to miss. Valluvar is not recommending spontaneous niceness but a deliberate search for what will actually benefit the hearer, delivered pleasantly. The two clauses form a causal pair with a striking agricultural logic: அல்லவை தேய ('evils wearing thin, eroding') and அறம் பெருகும் ('virtue swelling, increasing') — a single practice simultaneously depletes one and augments the other. This is one of the few places where Valluvar assigns speech a world-altering rather than merely personal effect, anticipating the argument of chapters 19 (on not slandering) and 20 (on avoiding useless words). The claim that gentle words can actually reduce the quantity of evil in the world finds its most dramatic mythic expression in Aeschylus and its clearest scriptural statement in Qur'an 41:34.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Patanjali prescribes that by deliberately cultivating friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the wicked, the mind becomes clear and undisturbed.
hinduism.explanation: The sutra treats chosen benevolent attitudes as a technique: adopting them dissolves the mental afflictions that generate harmful action.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's mechanism — deliberately sought-out goodwill erodes what is bad and increases what is good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase, but the sutra concerns inner attitudes and mental purification rather than speech and its social effects.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks for speech selected specifically for its capacity to build up the hearer — the negative rule and the positive purpose stated together.
christianity.tie_back: 'Good to the use of edifying' is the Kural's நல்லவை நாடி — seeking out what is genuinely good to say.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the deliberate selection of beneficial speech matches the Kural's naadi almost exactly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad deed. Repel [evil] by that which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an prescribes a better response as the active means of dissolving hostility, converting an enemy rather than defeating him.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim that evil wears away and good grows precisely through the better, gentler word.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sahih International; describes the transformation of enmity rather than a general increase of virtue, but the causal logic is the same.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud describes the person who studies Torah, is honest in business and speaks pleasantly with people: of such a one others say, 'happy is the father who taught him Torah — see how fine his ways are.' The one whose dealings and speech are unpleasant produces the opposite response, and thereby desecrates the divine Name.
judaism.explanation: Pleasant speech is treated as having public theological consequence: it makes holiness attractive, while harshness discredits it.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that pleasant, well-chosen speech visibly increases virtue in the world around the speaker.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verified passage; the frame is sanctification/desecration of the Name rather than a general account of virtue's increase.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He speaks words that are soothing to the ear, that are affectionate, that go to the heart, that are polite, appealing and pleasing to people at large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's positive definition of right speech to Cunda the silversmith, given as the direct replacement for abusive speech rather than merely its absence.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's programme exactly: abandoning harsh speech in favour of deliberately pleasing speech is what causes evil to decline and good to grow.
buddhism.source: Cunda Kammāraputta Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.176 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; the canonical positive statement of kindly speech in the Pali Canon.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I love the eyes of Persuasion, who guided my tongue and mouth against the fierce refusal of these deities.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At the close of the Oresteia, Athena wins over the vengeful Erinyes not by force but by Peitho (Persuasion); they are transformed into the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones, and the cycle of blood-vengeance ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim enacted on a civic scale: gentle words literally cause evil to wear away and blessing to increase.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides 970 (cf. 885) (trans. H. W. Smyth, rev. Bannon and Nagy)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified against the Center for Hellenic Studies text; a mythic dramatisation rather than a precept, but the transformation of evil by persuasion is exact.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates distinguishes the mere knack of flattery from a genuine art of rhetoric, which he defines as psychagōgia — a leading of souls — and argues that it is legitimate only when the speaker knows the truth and knows what will genuinely benefit the particular soul in front of him.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes the ethical worth of persuasive speech depend entirely on whether the speaker has sought out what is actually good for the hearer.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's நல்லவை நாடி — the prior search for what is genuinely good — made the precondition of legitimate speech.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of Plato's argument; his concern is the epistemology of rhetoric rather than the Kural's claim about virtue increasing in the world.

kurals.tamil:
நயன்ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும் பயன்ஈன்று
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayan eendru nandri payakkum payan eendru,
Panbin thalaippiriyaach chol.
kurals.meaning: Words that give real benefit to the hearer and never step outside the bounds of good character bring the speaker both goodwill in this life and moral merit.
kurals.elementary: There's a difference between a friend who tells you what you want to hear and a friend who tells you something helpful, kindly. The second kind of talking does two jobs at once: it helps the other person, and it makes you a better person too. This kural is about that double win.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a careful distinction between two returns: நயன் (nayan, goodwill, favour, social benefit accruing to the speaker) and நன்றி (nandri, here in its older sense of moral good or merit rather than gratitude). The condition for both is that the speech must be பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா — literally 'not parting from the head of good character' — a striking idiom implying that speech remains tethered to the speaker's cultivated disposition rather than floating free as mere technique. This anticipates by some centuries the point Aristotle makes about ethos, that the most potent mode of persuasion is the character the speech itself displays. The doubled ஈன்று (eendru, 'having borne/given birth to') repeated in both lines gives the verse a generative, almost obstetric image: beneficial speech reproduces itself as both goodwill and merit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita's four conditions — truthful, pleasing, beneficial, non-agitating — must all hold simultaneously; satisfying only some of them does not qualify.
hinduism.tie_back: 'Beneficial' (hita) and 'pleasing' (priya) held together is exactly the Kural's demand that speech yield real benefit without departing from good character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; the alignment of benefit with pleasantness is close to one-to-one with the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks for speech that is simultaneously gracious and substantive — salt being the ancient image for what preserves and gives savour, i.e. usefulness.
christianity.tie_back: Grace plus substance is the Kural's pairing of pleasantness with real benefit.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the 'salt' metaphor is usually read as usefulness or pointedness, which aligns well but is interpretively looser than the Kural's explicit payan.

islam.quote_or_event: “And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan induces [dissension] among them.”
islam.explanation: The instruction is comparative — not merely to say what is acceptable but to select what is best — and is immediately justified by the social damage that lesser speech causes.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's standard that speech must actively benefit rather than merely avoid offence.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sahih International; the command to say 'that which is best' is a strong match, though it does not address the speaker's own return.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs gives kind words a double effect: immediate sweetness to the spirit and actual restorative benefit to the body.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's twin yields — pleasantness and real benefit — are the honeycomb's sweetness and health.
judaism.source: Proverbs 16:24 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the benefit accrues to the hearer only, where the Kural also tracks the speaker's gain, and this is a Christian translation of the Tanakh.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathāgata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing and agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sets out a six-part grid of speech and will utter only what is both true and beneficial, adding pleasantness and timing as further filters — he will never say what is untrue or unbeneficial, however agreeable it might be.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's exact requirement: benefit and pleasantness together, never at the expense of good character.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; one of the most systematic treatments of the Kural's problem in any tradition.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Muses greet Hesiod on Helicon with the taunt that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, but also know, when they will, to utter true things — then breathe into him a divine voice and send him out to sing.
greek_mythology.explanation: The scene explicitly separates two capacities that sound identical from outside: persuasive falsehood and persuasive truth, with the poet's gift lying in the second.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's condition that pleasing speech must never part company with integrity.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate summary, but the passage concerns poetic authority rather than the ethics of everyday speech, so the connection is thematic only.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character when the speech is so spoken as to make us think him credible... We believe good men more fully and more readily than others.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle makes ethos one of the three proofs, insisting that the persuasive force resides in the character displayed by the speech itself, not in a reputation held independently of it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல் — speech that never departs from the speaker's good character — analysed as a technical principle.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Roberts translation, quoted with an ellipsis; Aristotle's interest is persuasive efficacy where Valluvar's is moral merit.

kurals.tamil:
சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல் மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்பம் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirumaiyul neengiya insol marumaiyum,
Immaiyum inbam tharum.
kurals.meaning: Kind words that carry no trace of meanness bring happiness both in this life and in the life to come.
kurals.elementary: Some people say something nice but slip a little insult inside it, like a stone hidden in a cake. This kural says the kind words that count are the ones with nothing mean tucked inside — and those are the ones that make you happy now and keep on paying you back later.
kurals.university: சிறுமை (sirumai) means smallness, and by extension pettiness, meanness or baseness; the phrase சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய ('having departed from smallness') therefore screens out the backhanded compliment, the sweetly delivered slight, the kindness offered as a display of superiority. Valluvar then makes his only eschatological claim in the chapter, invoking the standard Tamil pairing இம்மை / மறுமை (immai / marumai, this birth and the next). The pairing is significant for the Kural's interpretive history: it has been read by Jain scholars as evidence of a rebirth framework, by Saiva commentators as reference to heaven, and by twentieth-century secular readers as a rhetorical intensifier meaning simply 'always'. The formula 'in this world and the next' is one of the most durable rhetorical structures in world ethics, recurring near-verbatim in the Dhammapada, the Gita and the Mishnah.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna that the effort spent on good conduct is never wasted, in either of the two arenas of existence.
hinduism.tie_back: It uses the Kural's exact two-world structure to guarantee the durability of good action.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; the two-world promise matches exactly, but the subject is good action generally rather than speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus makes speech itself the basis of eschatological verdict, treating words as fully weighted moral acts rather than as incidental noise.
christianity.tie_back: It carries the Kural's speech into the next world as decisively as into this one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the two-world accountability of speech matches, though the emphasis falls on judgment rather than on the happiness the Kural promises.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes good speech a direct corollary of belief in the hereafter, placing every utterance inside the horizon of final accounting.
islam.tie_back: It links kind speech to the world to come precisely as the Kural does with marumai.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified against Sunnah.com; the hadith explicitly conditions speech on the Last Day, giving a tight match to the Kural's two-world frame.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists certain acts — honouring parents, deeds of loving-kindness, and making peace between people — as those whose fruits a person consumes in this world while the capital remains intact for the world to come.
judaism.explanation: The financial metaphor is precise: these acts pay a dividend immediately without depleting the principal reserved for the hereafter.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's double payoff — happiness in this life and the next — expressed as an accounting relationship.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as translations of the formula differ; 'making peace between people' is a speech act, but the list is broader than speech alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices. In both worlds the doer of good rejoices. He rejoices, he is exceedingly glad, seeing the purity of his own deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's twin verses set the wrongdoer and the doer of good in exact parallel, each receiving his result in both worlds.
buddhism.tie_back: Structurally and substantively the same promise the Kural makes for speech free of meanness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Buddharakkhita's wording; the two-world formula is near-identical, though the referent is meritorious deeds generally rather than speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod records that the righteous race of heroes was not extinguished but settled by Zeus at the ends of the earth on the Isles of the Blest beside deep-swirling Ocean, where the grain-giving earth bears honey-sweet fruit three times a year.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth does contain a picture of continued blessedness after death, but it is awarded for heroic worth and divine favour rather than for everyday moral conduct.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It offers the nearest Greek analogue to the Kural's marumai — happiness continuing past this life — without linking it to speech.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest weak match: Greek myth has no ethic of speech extending into the afterlife, so this is the best available structural analogue only.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates closes the Gorgias with a myth of judgment in which souls are stripped of body and reputation and judged naked, and argues from it that rhetoric is worth having only if it is used to serve justice, since the orator's own soul is what is finally at stake.
philosophy.explanation: Plato subordinates the entire question of persuasive speech to the speaker's condition in a post-mortem reckoning.
philosophy.tie_back: It reproduces the Kural's move of evaluating speech by its consequences in both this life and the next.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of the dialogue's closing argument; the concern is justice in oratory rather than kindness in ordinary speech.

kurals.tamil:
இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான் எவன்கொலோ
வன்சொல் வழங்கு வது.
kurals.transliteration:
Insol inidheendral kaanbaan evankolo,
Vansol vazhangu vadhu.
kurals.meaning: Someone who has seen for himself the pleasure kind words give — what on earth can he be thinking when he goes around dealing out harsh ones?
kurals.elementary: You already know how good it feels when someone is nice to you. So why would you ever be mean to someone else? You've already felt both sides. This kural is basically asking, with a raised eyebrow: what are you even doing?
kurals.university: This is the chapter's only rhetorical question, and Valluvar uses it for maximum force. எவன்கொலோ (evankolo) is an idiom of genuine puzzlement — 'whatever for?' — rather than condemnation, which makes the couplet feel less like a prohibition than an expression of bafflement. The argument's structure is a pure appeal to first-person evidence: the person addressed is a காண்பான், one who has himself seen and experienced the pleasure that kind words produce. Harsh speech is therefore presented not primarily as wicked but as irrational, a failure to reason from one's own experience to another's. This is precisely the logic of the Golden Rule in its negative form, and the verse's structure makes it the Kural's closest approach to that formula. The contrast pair இன்சொல் / வன்சொல் (sweet word / hard word) also sets up the culminating fruit-image of Kural 100.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arrogance, pride, anger, conceit, harshness and ignorance — these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists pāruṣya (harshness, especially harshness of speech) among the defining marks of the āsurī or demoniac disposition, in direct contrast to the divine qualities catalogued just before.
hinduism.tie_back: It names harsh speech itself as the disorder the Kural finds so inexplicable in someone who knows better.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; classifies harshness as a vice but does not reproduce the Kural's argument from personal experience.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs states the practical asymmetry: the gentle reply defuses a situation while the harsh one escalates it, so harshness is self-defeating.
christianity.tie_back: It supplies the answer to the Kural's question — there is no good reason for harsh words, since they only make matters worse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; one of the most direct parallels in the chapter, though framed as consequence rather than as a question about motive.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: Revealed after the reverse at Uhud, the verse tells the Prophet that his community held together because of his gentleness, and would have scattered had he been harsh.
islam.tie_back: It makes the Kural's point concretely: harsh speech destroys what gentle speech has built, so there is nothing to be gained by it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sahih International; the harsh/gentle contrast matches closely, in a leadership context rather than a general one.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yohanan taught in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai that the transgression of verbal mistreatment (ona'at devarim) is graver than that of monetary exploitation, because the one touches a person's very body while the other touches only his money — and the verse on verbal wronging alone concludes 'and you shall fear your God'.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis rank wounding words above financial fraud, on the reasoning that money is recoverable and dignity is not.
judaism.tie_back: It gives full weight to the harm the Kural's harsh speaker is inflicting without apparent reason.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verified passage; establishes the seriousness of harsh words but not the Kural's argument from experienced pleasure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada argues against harsh speech on grounds of reciprocity: the words you send out come back, and the cycle is unprofitable for everyone.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's puzzlement given an answer — harsh speech is simply a bad calculation by someone who already knows how words feel.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Buddharakkhita's wording; both the prohibition and the appeal to what the speaker himself will feel align closely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thersites, the only common soldier in the Iliad given a speaking part, is described as the ugliest man at Troy and an unmeasured, abusive railer who reviles the kings out of habit; Odysseus strikes him with the royal staff and the whole army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer draws Thersites as a man whose speech is harsh for no strategic reason at all, and the episode ends with his humiliation rather than any gain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the walking answer to the Kural's question: the habitual harsh speaker achieves nothing but his own diminishment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate summary; a cautionary figure rather than a stated principle, and Homer's treatment of Thersites carries class assumptions the Kural does not share.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and vexation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and vexed.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius, in his list of remedies against anger, points out that the reaction consistently costs more than the provocation did.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the missing calculation behind the Kural's question: dealing out harsh words costs the speaker more than it could ever return.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified in Long's translation; addresses anger's cost generally rather than harsh speech specifically.

kurals.tamil:
இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்
கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Iniya ulavaaga innaadha kooral,
Kani iruppak kaaikavarn dhatru.
kurals.meaning: To speak hurtful words when pleasant ones are right there for the taking is like grabbing at the unripe fruit while the ripe fruit hangs beside it.
kurals.elementary: Picture a tree with sweet ripe mangoes hanging low and hard green ones next to them. Nobody would reach past the sweet ones to bite a sour green one. But that's exactly what people do when they say something harsh when a kind thing would have worked just as well.
kurals.university: The chapter closes on its most famous image, and the comparison is chosen with care: கனி (kani, ripe fruit) and காய் (kaai, unripe fruit) come from the same tree at the same moment, so the choice costs nothing and requires no extra effort — which is exactly the point. உளவாக (ulavaaga, 'there being available') carries the weight: the pleasant words are already present and to hand. The verse thus completes the chapter's argument by removing the last excuse, since harsh speech can no longer be defended as necessary, cheaper, or more efficient. The kani/kaai contrast belongs to a wider Tamil poetic register of fruit imagery, and the comparative particle அற்று (atru, 'is like that') is the classical Tamil marker of simile. Strikingly, three other traditions independently reach for fruit or tree imagery at exactly this point — James on the fig and the vine, the Qur'an on the good and evil tree, Proverbs on apples of gold — suggesting how naturally the ethics of speech attracts the metaphor of cultivation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not, even though in pain, (speak words) cutting (others) to the quick; let him not injure others in thought or deed; let him not utter speeches which make (others) afraid of him, since that will prevent him from gaining heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu rules out cutting speech even under the one circumstance that might seem to excuse it — the speaker's own suffering — and attaches an eschatological penalty.
hinduism.tie_back: It removes the excuse for harsh words just as the Kural does, on the ground that nothing is gained by them.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 2.161 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Bühler; a prohibition on harsh speech rather than the Kural's specific argument that the pleasant alternative is freely available.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter? Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh.”
christianity.explanation: James's discourse on the tongue uses agricultural and hydrological images to argue that sweet and bitter speech cannot legitimately issue from the same source.
christianity.tie_back: It reaches for exactly the Kural's register — fruit, sweetness, bitterness — to make the same point about the incoherence of choosing the bitter.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the fruit imagery and the subject (the tongue) match well, though James argues about consistency rather than about a freely available choice.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky? It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord... And the example of a bad word is like a bad tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, not having any stability.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets the good word and the bad word side by side as two trees, one endlessly fruitful and rooted, the other torn up and worthless.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's ripe-fruit / unripe-fruit choice extended into a full arboreal parable.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sahih International, quoted with an ellipsis; an unusually close match of both subject and imagery.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs values the well-chosen word by comparing it to precious fruit set in a worked silver frame — something both beautiful and deliberately fashioned.
judaism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's fruit-metaphor for the well-chosen word, treating the good option as the obviously superior one.
judaism.source: Proverbs 25:11 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV; the shared fruit imagery is striking but Proverbs praises the good word without contrasting it against the available bad one, and this is a Christian rendering of the Tanakh.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha sorts people into three kinds by their speech: those whose speech is like dung, those whose speech is like flowers, and those whose speech is like honey — the last being the person whose words are gentle, pleasing to the ear and spoken with affection.
buddhism.explanation: The image deliberately ranges from the repulsive to the delicious, making the choice between them look as obvious as a choice between foods.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same sensory-appetite logic as the Kural's ripe-versus-unripe fruit: nobody deliberately chooses the worse thing to consume.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Sutta identity and content verified; given as paraphrase because a published verbatim English rendering was not confirmed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod, in the practical wisdom that closes Works and Days, ranks a measured tongue as a man's chief asset and notes that abuse simply returns amplified.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reaches the Kural's conclusion by the same practical route: the harsh option is plainly the worse buy.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719–721 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Evelyn-White; gnomic wisdom rather than myth proper, and it praises restraint where the Kural praises sweetness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is pleasant in the right way is friendly and the mean is friendliness, while the man who exceeds is an obsequious person if he has no end in view, a flatterer if he is aiming at his own advantage, and the man who falls short and is unpleasant in all circumstances is a quarrelsome and surly sort of person.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle constructs a virtue of everyday social pleasantness, positioned between the flatterer who gives pleasure dishonestly and the churl who gives pain for no reason at all.
philosophy.tie_back: His 'quarrelsome and surly' person is precisely the Kural's fruit-picker who reaches past the ripe for the green.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.6, 1126b (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; Aristotle analyses the vice structurally where Valluvar diagnoses it as simple bad judgment.
